18.01.title: Measurement uncertainty
18.01.html:
A measurement without an uncertainty is only half a result. “The flow is 7.3 L/s” says little. “7.3 L/s, 95 % interval 3.5 to 12.1 L/s” tells the reader whether the number can support a decision. The international rulebook is the GUM, the Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (JCGM 100:2008).

Standard uncertainty: type A and type B

Every input xi​ gets a standard uncertainty u(xi​), the standard deviation of what you believe about it. The GUM names two ways to get it:

  • Type A, from statistics of repeated readings. For n readings with sample standard deviation s, the uncertainty of the mean is u=s/n​.
  • Type B, from anything else: a resolution, a calibration certificate, a tolerance. If all you know is that the value lies within ±a, a rectangular distribution gives u=a/3​.

Both kinds are then treated the same way. The labels say how you got the number, not how much you trust it.

Propagation by linearisation

For a result y=f(x1​,…,xN​) with independent inputs, a first-order Taylor expansion gives the combined standard uncertainty

uc2​(y)=i=1∑N​ci2​u2(xi​),ci​=∂xi​∂f​.

The ci​ are sensitivity coefficients, and each term ci2​u2(xi​)/uc2​ is that input’s share of the uncertainty budget. For a power law y=x1a​x2b​, this reduces to relative uncertainties: (uc​/y)2=a2(u1​/x1​)2+b2(u2​/x2​)2. The expanded uncertainty U=kuc​ with k=2 gives roughly a 95 % interval when the result is close to normal.

Propagation by Monte Carlo

GUM Supplement 1 skips the Taylor series. Draw M samples of every input from its distribution, push each set through f, and read the mean, the standard deviation and the 2.5 % and 97.5 % percentiles of the results. It costs a few hundred thousand function calls and needs no derivatives. When f is close to linear over ±2u of its inputs, both methods agree. When it is not, Monte Carlo is the one to believe.

Worked exampleg from a pendulum, then a weir that breaks linearisation

Pendulum. Ten stopwatch readings of 20 swings: 40.13, 40.21, 40.08, 40.17, 40.25, 40.11, 40.19, 40.06, 40.22, 40.15 s. The length to the bob centre is L=1.000 m ±2 mm (tape measure).

  1. Period T=2.00785 s. Type A: u=0.00099 s. Add the 0.01 s stopwatch resolution as type B, 0.01/3​/20, to get u(T)=0.00103 s.
  2. u(L)=0.002/3​=0.00115 m.
  3. g=4π2L/T2=9.7926 m/s². Sensitivities: ∂g/∂L=9.7926 s⁻², ∂g/∂T=−2g/T=−9.7543 m/s³.
  4. uc​=0.0151 m/s², so g=9.793±0.030 m/s² (k=2). The budget is 56 % length and 44 % period: a better tape measure helps as much as more timing.
  5. Monte Carlo with 400 000 samples: mean 9.7926, u=0.0151, 95 % interval [9.7639, 9.8214]. The methods agree to better than 1 %. The local value in Zurich, 9.807 m/s², is inside the interval.

Weir. Q=32​Cd​b2g​h1.5 with Cd​=0.62±0.02, b=0.50 m ±5 mm, and a small head h=40±8 mm (ripples on the staff gauge).

  1. Linearised: Q=7.323 L/s, U=4.420 L/s, interval [2.903, 11.744] L/s.
  2. Monte Carlo: mean 7.434 L/s and 95 % interval [3.465, 12.088] L/s. Because h1.5 is convex, the mean is biased 1.5 % upwards and the interval reaches 4.77 L/s above the estimate but only 3.86 L/s below it. Linearisation cannot see either effect. Report the Monte Carlo interval, and if the decision matters, measure the head in a stilling well.

Exercise 1The budget of a density measurement

A steel cylinder has mass m=245.3±0.1 g, diameter d=25.00±0.02 mm and length L=64.00±0.05 mm (all standard uncertainties). Find ρ=4m/(πd2L), its relative uncertainty and the biggest term in the budget.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ρ=4×0.2453/(π×0.0252×0.064)=7808 kg/m³.
  2. Power law with exponents 1, −2, −1: (u/ρ)2=(0.1/245.3)2+(2×0.02/25)2+(0.05/64)2.
  3. Terms: (4.08×10−4)2, (1.60×10−3)2, (7.81×10−4)2. Sum 3.34×10−6, so u/ρ=0.183 %, u=14 kg/m³.
  4. The diameter dominates (77 % of the budget) because it enters squared. Measure it at several positions and use a better micrometer.

18.02.title: Sensors and transducers
18.02.html:
A transducer turns the quantity you care about into one you can measure, usually a voltage. A thermocouple turns temperature into microvolts, a piezo crystal turns force into charge, and a strain gauge turns stretch into a tiny change of resistance. This lesson takes the strain gauge apart, because the same bridge circuit sits inside load cells, pressure sensors and torque meters.

The strain gauge

A foil gauge is a zig-zag of thin metal on a plastic backing, glued to the part. Stretch it by strain ε and its resistance changes:

RΔR​=GFε,

with the gauge factor GF≈2 for constantan foil. At 1000 µε (a steel part at about 200 MPa) a 350 Ω gauge changes by only 0.74 Ω. You cannot read that with an ohmmeter while it drifts with temperature, so you put the gauge in a bridge.

The Wheatstone bridge

Four arms R1​,R2​,R3​,R4​ form two voltage dividers across the excitation V. The output is the difference of the two mid-points:

Vout​=V(R1​+R2​R1​​−R3​+R4​R4​​).

With all four equal the bridge is balanced and Vout​=0, whatever V is. Write Ri​=R(1+xi​) with small xi​ and expand to first order:

Vout​≈4V​(x1​−x2​+x3​−x4​).

Opposite arms add and adjacent arms subtract. That one line explains every bridge configuration:

  • Quarter bridge: one active gauge, x1​=GFε. Exactly, Vout​=Vx/(4+2x), so Vout​≈VGFε/4 with a non-linearity of about x/2.
  • Half bridge on a bending beam: gauges on top (+ε) and bottom (−ε) in adjacent arms. Vout​=VGFε/2 exactly, twice the signal.
  • Full bridge: four active gauges, Vout​=VGFε.

Temperature makes every gauge on the part read the same apparent strain. In adjacent arms it cancels, so a half bridge, or a quarter bridge with an unstrained dummy gauge in the adjacent arm, is temperature-compensated.

Worked exampleA 350 Ω gauge at 1000 µε

GF=2.1, V=5 V, so x=GFε=0.0021.

  1. Quarter bridge. Exact Vout​=5×0.0021/(4+0.0042)=2.62225 mV. The linear formula gives 2.62500 mV, a non-linearity of 0.105 %. It grows to 0.52 % at 5000 µε and 1.04 % at 10 000 µε.
  2. Half bridge: 5.25000 mV, full bridge: 10.50000 mV, with no non-linearity at all.
  3. Temperature. Warm the part by 10 K with 1.5 µε/K of apparent strain. The quarter bridge drifts by 39.4 µV, which looks like 15 µε of load. With a dummy gauge or in a half bridge the drift is zero.
  4. Lead wires. 10 m of 0.14 mm² copper each way adds RL​=2.50 Ω in series with the gauge. That desensitises the quarter bridge by RL​/(R+RL​)=0.71 %. A three-wire connection puts one lead in each adjacent arm and cancels most of it.

Exercise 1Size the amplifier

A full bridge with GF=2.0, V=10 V carries ±500 µε at full load. You want ±2.5 V into an ADC. What gain do you need, and what is the bridge output per µε?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Full bridge: Vout​=VGFε=10×2.0×500×10−6=10 mV at full load.
  2. Gain =2.5/0.010=250.
  3. Sensitivity 10×2.0×10−6=20 µV per µε before the amplifier, 5 mV per µε after it.

18.03.title: Sampling and aliasing
18.03.html:
A data logger does not record a signal. It records a list of numbers, one every Ts​=1/fs​ seconds. Between the samples it knows nothing, and that ignorance has a precise and dangerous consequence: two different signals can produce the same samples.

Why sines can impersonate each other

Sample x(t)=sin(2πft) at tn​=n/fs​. Replace f by f+kfs​ for any integer k:

sin(2π(f+kfs​)n/fs​)=sin(2πfn/fs​+2πkn)=sin(2πfn/fs​).

The samples are identical. Also sin(2π(fs​−f)n/fs​)=−sin(2πfn/fs​), the same sine with a sign flip. So every frequency folds into the band 0≤f≤fs​/2, and a component at f shows up at the alias

fa​=​f−fs​round(fs​f​)​.

The Nyquist-Shannon theorem

If the signal contains nothing at or above fs​/2 (the Nyquist frequency), the samples determine it completely, and sinc interpolation rebuilds it exactly. If it does contain energy above fs​/2, no processing after the fact can tell it from a real low-frequency component. Hence the rule of every data-acquisition system: put an analogue anti-aliasing filter in front of the ADC, and sample several times faster than the highest frequency you care about.

The wagon-wheel effect

A film camera samples a moving picture. A wheel with N identical spokes looks the same every 1/N of a turn, so the picture repeats at the spoke frequency Nfrot​. If that is above half the frame rate it aliases. The eye follows the nearest spoke, and the wheel appears to turn at

fapp​=NNfrot​−fs​round(Nfrot​/fs​)​,

which can be slow, zero or negative.

Worked exampleA vibration logger and a car on film

Logger. A 200 Hz logger with a 1024-point FFT and a Hann window. The code builds the FFT from scratch and checks it against np.fft.fft.

True frequency, Hz FFT peak, Hz Alias formula, Hz
30 29.998 30
110 89.997 90
180 20.002 20
230 29.998 30
397 3.003 3

A 180 Hz gear-mesh vibration reads as a convincing 20 Hz peak. Nothing in the data says it is fake.

Car. A 6-spoke rim, tyre diameter 0.63 m, at 50 km/h, filmed at 25 frames per second.

  1. frot​=(50/3.6)/(π×0.63)=7.0174 rev/s. Spoke frequency 6×7.0174=42.104 Hz, above the 12.5 Hz Nyquist limit.
  2. 42.104−25×2=−7.896 Hz, divided by 6 spokes: the wheel seems to turn backwards at 1.3159 rev/s. Tracking the nearest spoke frame by frame in the code gives the same number.
  3. It looks frozen whenever Nfrot​ is a multiple of 25 Hz: at 29.69 km/h and 59.38 km/h.

Exercise 1Choose a sampling rate

A pump runs at 1450 rpm with 7 impeller vanes. You want to see the blade-pass frequency and its second harmonic without aliasing. What is the minimum sampling rate, and what would a 250 Hz logger show instead of the blade-pass tone?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Shaft 1450/60=24.17 Hz. Blade-pass 7×24.17=169.2 Hz, second harmonic 338.3 Hz.
  2. Nyquist needs fs​>2×338.3=676.7 Hz. In practice use 1 kHz or more with an anti-aliasing filter at about 400 Hz.
  3. At 250 Hz: ∣169.2−250∣=80.8 Hz. The logger shows an 80.8 Hz tone that does not exist.

18.04.title: Filters
18.04.html:
Real sensor signals carry noise: mains hum at 50 Hz, vibration from a motor, electronic hiss. A low-pass filter keeps the slow part you care about and removes the fast part. In code a filter is a difference equation, a few multiplications per sample, and the whole design job is choosing its coefficients.

The RC filter

A resistor in series with a capacitor, output across the capacitor:

RCy˙​+y=x⟹H(s)=1+sRC1​,∣H(jω)∣=1+(ωRC)2​1​.

The cutoff fc​=1/(2πRC) is where ∣H∣=1/2​ (−3 dB). Above it the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. That is gentle: a tone at 5fc​ is only reduced to 0.196.

Butterworth: as flat as possible

The n-th order Butterworth filter has ∣H(jω)∣2=1/(1+(ω/ωc​)2n), maximally flat in the passband and falling by 20n dB per decade. For n=2:

H(s)=s2+2​ωc​s+ωc2​ωc2​​.

From s to a difference equation: the bilinear transform

Sampling at fs​ with period T, replace s by

s=T2​z+1z−1​,

where z−1 means “one sample ago”. This maps the stable left half-plane exactly into the unit circle, so a stable analogue filter stays stable. It also squeezes the infinite analogue frequency axis into 0≤f<fs​/2: an analogue frequency ωa​ lands at ωa​=(2/T)tan(ωd​T/2). Pre-warping sets K=tan(πfc​/fs​) so the cutoff lands where you asked. For the second-order Butterworth:

yn​=b0​xn​+b1​xn−1​+b2​xn−2​−a1​yn−1​−a2​yn−2​,
b0​=b2​=a0′​K2​,b1​=2b0​,a1​=a0′​2(K2−1)​,a2​=a0′​1−2​K+K2​,a0′​=1+2​K+K2.

The resulting digital magnitude is exactly 1/1+(tan(πf/fs​)/K)4​, slightly better than the analogue prototype near Nyquist.

Worked exampleClean an accelerometer signal

fs​=500 Hz, fc​=10 Hz, second-order Butterworth.

  1. K=tan(π⋅10/500)=0.062915. Coefficients: b0​=b2​=0.00362168, b1​=0.00724336, a1​=−1.82269493, a2​=0.83718165. Both poles have ∣z∣=0.914976<1, so the filter is stable.
  2. Gains: 0.999205 at 2 Hz, 0.707107 at 10 Hz, and 0.037467 (−28.53 dB) at 50 Hz. The analogue prototype gives 0.039968 at 50 Hz: the bilinear warping helps here.
  3. Running the difference equation on 10 s of the noisy signal, a least-squares fit of the output tones gives gains 0.9992 at 2 Hz and 0.0374 at 50 Hz, matching ∣H∣.
  4. The price is phase lag: 16.40° at 2 Hz, a 22.77 ms delay. For a controller that delay matters (lesson 18.13). For offline analysis, running the filter forwards and then backwards cancels the phase.
  5. A first-order RC with the same cutoff only reduces the 50 Hz tone to 0.1901.
  6. With SciPy installed, the coefficients match scipy.signal.butter(2, 10, fs=500) and the output matches scipy.signal.lfilter to rounding error.

Exercise 1An RC filter in hardware

You want a 100 Hz RC low-pass in front of an ADC with a 10 kΩ resistor. What capacitor do you need, and how much does the filter attenuate a 1 kHz component?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. C=1/(2πRfc​)=1/(2π×104×100)=159 nF. Use the standard 150 nF, giving fc​=106 Hz.
  2. At 1 kHz with fc​=100 Hz: ∣H∣=1/1+102​=0.0995, about −20 dB.
  3. One decade above the cutoff gives only a factor of 10. If 1 kHz noise must not alias, use a higher-order filter or a faster ADC.

18.05.title: Data acquisition with microcontrollers
18.05.html:
A microcontroller board, an Arduino, an ESP32 or a Raspberry Pi Pico, turns a sensor voltage into numbers and sends them to a laptop over USB serial. For a few euros it is a data logger good enough for most lab work, if you know what its analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) can and cannot resolve.

Resolution and the quantisation step

An N-bit ADC with reference voltage Vref​ maps 0…Vref​ onto the integer codes 0…2N−1. One code is a step of

q=2NVref​​.

An Arduino Uno (10 bits, 5 V) has q=4.883 mV. An ESP32 or a Pico (12 bits, 3.3 V) has 0.806 mV, though their real accuracy is worse than the bit count suggests.

Quantisation noise

Rounding to the nearest code makes an error e between −q/2 and +q/2. For a busy signal that crosses many codes, e is uniformly distributed, and its standard deviation is

σe​=q1​∫−q/2q/2​e2de​=12​q​.

For a full-scale sine of amplitude 2N−1q, the signal power is (2N−1q)2/2, which gives the classic

SNR=10log10​q2/12(2N−1q)2/2​=6.02N+1.76 dB.

Averaging and dither

Averaging M readings reduces random noise by M​. But if the analogue signal is quieter than one step, every reading returns the same code and averaging changes nothing. Some noise of about q rms, called dither, spreads the readings over neighbouring codes, and then the average does resolve finer than q. Oversampling with dither is how cheap ADCs buy extra bits.

A logger you can trust

Serial lines get corrupted: a loose USB cable, a reset mid-line. Each line should carry a checksum so the laptop can reject bad lines instead of logging garbage. The firmware below sends t_ms,ax,ay,az*CS, where CS is the XOR of all bytes before the *, in hex (the NMEA convention used by GPS receivers).

Worked exampleQuantisation noise and an accelerometer at rest

  1. Quantisation noise. For 200 000 random voltages, the rms rounding error is 1.4116 mV at 10 bits and 5 V, against the theory value q/12​=1.4095 mV. At 12 bits and 3.3 V it is 0.2329 mV against 0.2326 mV.
  2. SNR. A full-scale sine through the 10-bit ADC gives 61.99 dB, against 6.02×10+1.76=61.96 dB.
  3. Accelerometer. An ADXL335 on 3.3 V gives 0.33 V/g with 1.65 V at 0 g. On an Uno one code is 4.883/0.33=14.80 mg.
  4. Quiet sensor (0.2 mV rms noise): every reading is the same code. Averaging 64 readings leaves a 1.18 mg bias, the distance from 1.65 V to the nearest code, and no spread.
  5. Noisy sensor (4 mV rms, about q): the readings spread over 7 codes, and averages of 64 have a bias of only 0.15 mg with a spread of 1.48 mg. The noise made the average better.
  6. Logger. The code parses 200 lines from a simulated board, rejects the one corrupted line (its checksum fails), and saves 199 rows to accel_log.csv. The mean of the z channel is 1.007 g, which is gravity to within one step.

Honest note: no board was connected to the machine that built this course, so the lesson numbers come from the simulated stream. Run python daq.py --port /dev/ttyACM0 (Windows: COM3) with pyserial installed to log your own board. The same parser and checks apply.

Exercise 1Is 10 bits enough?

You want to measure a bridge output of 0 to 20 mV with 0.1 % of full-scale resolution. The Uno’s ADC has 5 V range and 10 bits. What gain do you need in front of it, and is 10 bits enough?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 0.1 % of full scale needs at least 1000 steps across the range. 10 bits gives 1024, which is just enough if the signal fills the whole range.
  2. Gain to map 20 mV to 5 V: 5/0.020=250.
  3. Then one step is 4.883 mV/250=19.5 µV at the bridge, 0.098 % of 20 mV. In practice use a 24-bit bridge ADC such as the HX711 and skip the amplifier.

18.06.title: River flow measurement
18.06.html:
How much water does a canal carry? In Bali the answer decides how a subak shares water between terraces. In Zurich the Federal Office for the Environment publishes the Limmat’s discharge every ten minutes. Both rest on the same idea: discharge is velocity times area, added up over the cross-section.

The velocity-area method

Discharge is the flux of velocity through the cross-section A:

Q=∫A​udA≈i∑​vˉi​Ai​.

Divide the section into panels with verticals at positions yi​. At each one, measure the depth di​ with a wading rod and the depth-mean velocity vˉi​ with a current meter. The mid-section method (ISO 748) gives each vertical a panel reaching halfway to its neighbours:

Q=i∑​vˉi​di​wi​,wi​=2yi+1​−yi−1​​,

with the banks as the end points. ISO 748 asks for at least 20 verticals, with no panel carrying more than 10 % of the flow.

Where to hold the meter: the 0.6-depth rule

In a rough channel the velocity grows from the bed roughly as a power law, u=us​(z/d)1/m with m≈7. Its depth-mean is

vˉ=d1​∫0d​us​(dz​)1/7dz=87​us​,

and the profile takes that value at z/d=(7/8)7=0.39. So a single reading at 0.6 of the depth below the surface (0.4 above the bed) gives the mean velocity. The 0.2/0.8 two-point method is more robust when the profile is not a clean power law.

The float method

With no current meter, time an orange or a stick over a known length L. That gives the surface velocity L/t, so multiply by a coefficient k=vˉ/us​. For the 1/7 profile k=0.875; field guides quote 0.8 to 0.9 depending on depth and roughness. The uncertainty in k usually dominates the error, so the float method is a 5 to 10 % method at best.

Worked exampleGauge an irrigation canal

The canal is 3 m wide with a parabolic bed, 0.8 m deep at the centre, and a surface velocity of 0.9 m/s at the centre that falls towards the banks as (d/D)2/3.

  1. Exact. The area is 2BD/3=1.6 m², and integrating 87​us​d across the section gives Q=1.07465 m³/s.
  2. 0.6-depth rule. 0.41/7=0.87731, within 0.3 % of 0.875.
  3. Current meter, depths read to 5 mm and velocities with 2 % scatter:
Verticals Mid-section Q, m³/s Error Floats, k=0.85, m³/s Error
5 1.0501 −2.28 % 1.0258 −4.55 %
10 1.0676 −0.66 % 1.0407 −3.16 %
20 1.0797 +0.47 % 1.0591 −1.45 %
  1. With perfect readings at 20 verticals the method gives 1.07664 m³/s (+0.19 %), so the remaining error is the instruments, not the method.
  2. The floats carry a systematic −2.9 % error because the textbook k=0.85 is not this canal’s 0.875. Random timing errors average out over many verticals; that bias does not.

Exercise 1Gauge a ditch with oranges

A rectangular ditch is 1.2 m wide and 0.35 m deep. Three oranges take 12.4, 11.8 and 12.9 s to float 8 m down the centre. Estimate the discharge with k=0.85, and say what limits the result.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Mean time 12.37 s, surface velocity 8/12.37=0.647 m/s.
  2. Mean velocity 0.85×0.647=0.550 m/s. Area 1.2×0.35=0.42 m².
  3. Q≈0.231 m³/s, about 230 L/s.
  4. The oranges ran down the centre, the fastest part of the ditch, so the sidewalls make the real mean lower. With k only known within about ±10 %, quote Q=0.23±0.03 m³/s.

18.07.title: Strain and force measurement
18.07.html:
A kitchen scale, a crane’s overload sensor and a bicycle power meter all use the same trick: let the force bend a piece of metal a little, measure the strain with gauges in a bridge, and calibrate the result against known weights. This lesson designs a 5 kg bending-beam load cell and calibrates it.

The bending-beam load cell

A cantilever of width b and thickness h carries the force F at a distance a from the gauges. The bending moment there is M=Fa, and the surface strain is

ε=EIM(h/2)​=Ebh26Fa​.

Put two gauges on top (+ε) and two underneath (−ε) in a full bridge (lesson 18.02). The output is Vout​/V=GFε, usually quoted in mV/V: a cell rated at 2 mV/V gives 10 mV at full load on 5 V excitation. Design for about 1000 µε at rated load: enough signal, and a stress far below yield so the beam returns to zero and survives overloads.

Calibration by least squares

Beam theory predicts the sensitivity within a few per cent, but gauge position, glue and the beam’s real thickness change it, so every cell is calibrated. Apply known masses mi​, read the outputs ri​, and fit r=r0​+Sm by least squares:

[r0​S​]=(ATA)−1ATr,A=​1⋮1​m1​⋮mn​​​.

The residual standard deviation s gives the parameter covariance s2(ATA)−1, which feeds the uncertainty of every later reading.

The numbers on a datasheet

  • Linearity error: the largest deviation of the calibration points from the best-fit straight line, as a percentage of full scale (% FS).
  • Hysteresis: the largest difference between the loading and unloading readings at the same load, as % FS.
  • Zero and sensitivity, with their uncertainties.

Commercial cells of OIML class C3 are within about 0.02 % FS on each.

Worked exampleDesign and calibrate a 5 kg cell

Design. Aluminium 6061-T6 (E=69 GPa, yield 276 MPa), b=12.7 mm, a=60 mm, F=5×9.81=49.05 N.

  1. For 1000 µε, h=6Fa/(Ebε)​=4.489 mm. Choose 4.5 mm: ε=995.1 µε, stress 68.7 MPa, a factor of 4.02 on yield.
  2. Full bridge with GF=2.0: 1.9902 mV/V. On 5 V excitation that predicts 1.99019 mV/kg.

Calibration. Masses 0 to 5 kg in 1 kg steps up and back down, read with an amplifier noise of 0.4 µV.

  1. Least squares: sensitivity 1.98988 mV/kg ± 0.00049, within 0.02 % of the beam-theory prediction, and zero 9.75 µV.
  2. Residual standard deviation 2.57 µV. Linearity error 0.039 % FS, hysteresis 0.047 % FS: about class C3.
  3. Use. A reading of 4.21 mV gives (4.21−r0​)/S=2.1108 kg. Propagating the fit covariance and the residual scatter gives ±2.7 g (k=2).

Exercise 1Make it a 50 kg cell

Keep b and a and the 1000 µε target. How thick must the beam be for 50 kg, and what happens to the safety factor on yield?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. h∝F​, so h=4.489×10​=14.20 mm.
  2. The design strain is the same 1000 µε, so the stress is again Eε=69 MPa and the factor on yield stays about 4.
  3. A thicker beam is stiffer: its deflection scales as Fa3/(Ebh3), so the 50 kg cell deflects 10/101.5=0.32 times as much as the 5 kg cell at full load.

18.08.title: Temperature measurement
18.08.html:
A thermometer only tells you its own temperature. It reads the fluid correctly only after it has caught up with it, and a fast-changing temperature is always read late and smoothed. Knowing the sensor’s time constant turns that from a hidden error into a number you can correct for.

The first-order sensor

Treat the sensor tip as a lump of mass m and specific heat c, exchanging heat with the fluid through a surface A with coefficient h (lesson 13.06). An energy balance gives

mcdtdTs​​=hA(T−Ts​)⟹τdtdTs​​+Ts​=T,τ=hAmc​.

For a spherical bead of diameter d, τ=ρcd/(6h). The same sensor is fast in stirred water (h≈2000 W/m²K) and slow in still air (h≈10 to 100).

Step and ramp responses

Plunge the probe from T0​ into a bath at T∞​ at time t0​:

Ts​(t)=T∞​−(T∞​−T0​)e−(t−t0​)/τ.

After one τ it has covered 63.2 % of the step, after 3τ 95 %, after 5τ 99.3 %. If the fluid instead warms at a steady rate R, the sensor settles to the same rate but lags by Rτ kelvin: a 1.5 s probe in an oven ramping at 5 K/min reads 0.125 K low, for ever.

Identifying τ

  1. The 63.2 % point. Easy, but it needs t0​ and T∞​ and uses two noisy samples.
  2. Log-linear least squares. ln((T∞​−Ts​)/(T∞​−T0​))=−(t−t0​)/τ is a straight line: fit it over, say, 10 % to 95 % of the rise, where the logarithm is not dominated by noise.
  3. Non-linear least squares. Fit all four parameters (T∞​,T0​,τ,t0​) by Gauss-Newton: linearise the model around the current guess, solve the linear least-squares problem JΔp=r, update, repeat. It uses every sample and gives an uncertainty from s2(JTJ)−1.

Worked examplePlunge test of a sheathed probe

A 3 mm sheathed thermocouple at 22 °C is plunged into water at 80 °C at t0​=0.37 s. The synthetic data have τ=1.50 s and 0.15 K noise, sampled at 20 Hz for 12 s.

  1. 63.2 % time: τ=1.525 s (+1.7 %).
  2. Log-linear fit: τ=1.493 s (−0.5 %), t0​=0.374 s.
  3. Gauss-Newton from the log-linear start, 4 iterations: τ=1.5011±0.0025 s (+0.07 %), T∞​=80.016, T0​=21.988, t0​=0.3700 s.
  4. All three are within the 5 % target. The non-linear fit is about 7 times closer than the log-linear one because it uses all 240 samples.
  5. Bead sizes with ρc=8700×450 J/(m³K): a 0.5 mm bead has τ=0.163 s in stirred water and 3.26 s in moving air. The sheathed probe is slower than its size suggests because the insulation between wire and sheath adds a thermal resistance the lumped bead formula ignores.
  6. Ramp lag: at 5 K/min this probe reads 0.125 K behind. A simulation of the ODE confirms it.

Exercise 1Correct for the lag

A probe with τ=2.0 s reads 51.3 °C and is rising at 0.6 K/s. Estimate the fluid temperature now. Why is this correction dangerous on noisy data?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. From τT˙s​+Ts​=T: T=51.3+2.0×0.6=52.5 °C.
  2. The correction uses the derivative of the reading, and differentiating amplifies noise: 0.1 K of noise between samples 0.05 s apart is 2 K/s of slope, or 4 K of error after multiplying by τ. Filter first (lesson 18.04), or use a faster sensor.
